spoken_segments.text: Hey guys, I'm Thariq. Nice to meet you. Yeah, I wanted to talk to you about a couple things I've been thinking about since I left Anthropic.
It's been a wild year and there are a bunch of reflections I've had.
And my conclusion is about what I'm calling the sweet side of the bitter lesson. And the ways I've been wrong.

spoken_segments.text: So, I think I got a lot of things right this year.
I think I was right about models being able to edit and generate videos. I was talking about this like sometime in like June last year.

And I was right about models being able to help you understand and figure out your unknowns, to help like plan and learn about things. So, these are all things I was like right about and I was happy and I think that like a lot of you might be incorporating this sort of stuff in your work.

He scrolls through `tune` parameters (`seconds`, `metres`, `metresPerSecond`, `share`), `run()`, and `fromTheGround()`, then edits a tuning value on line 16 (`throwWeight` / `size` area) to `metres(1.5)`? spoken_segments.text: Okay, so this is my game. I've got in here this folder `game`. And then I've got here this code. This is the like agent code, right? Like this is the code where I'm like dude I don't know how, you know, cameras work or whatever.

But then in this code I have all my characters and I have their abilities. And so I can go in here and I can say like, okay. This is the rock move, right? Um, and inside of this move there's a bunch of ways to tune it. Um, it's well commented. It uses things like meters, you know what I mean? Instead of like X like .5 or whatever. Um, it tries to like create a bunch of different abstractions along the way.

And so I can see that like one of the things that, you know, is useful is that like there are three ways for this character to throw a rock, right? Like it can grab it from the ground, it can grab it from the wall or something. Um, and I can see sort of like the true logic of the character, right? I don't really know how the engine works or how, you know, this is implemented underneath, but I've essentially created this like almost a custom scripting language for my game.

And so that means like, you know, when I'm playing this game, um I can tweak little things. You know, I'm still like working on it. So like I can say I want the rock to be a lot bigger so I can say like, um, you know, 1.5, but using an actual IDE.

spoken_segments.text: And so, I think the takeaway for me has been that like I now have to think about the best way for me to deliver high quality software, right? spoken_segments.text: And, you know, I think many people have talked today at this conference about how to be more ambitious and I don't think any of this is quite new. But I just think there's like many things to do, like new languages, right? Like obviously, like, you know, uh, we want things like Rust that are very efficient, but we also want things to be, uh, potentially modular and like hot reloadable. Um, we want it to be potentially readable, right?

Uh, new primitives, like there are probably new types of databases, new types of servers, like, um, new operating system interactions—I've been sort of like vibe coding a bunch of personal software, um, that sort of messes with my operating system. Uh, there are new interaction paradigms possible, I think. Um, a lot of like old HCI research is now like very interesting to revisit. Um, new aesthetics, I think the way that we like use and design software can change quite a lot.
And um yeah, I think that like there's so much to do here that I don't think any of this—everyone, every speaker I think has talked about this. And um I don't have too much more to add.

spoken_segments.text: But I think that like what I really want us to say is that what we need to do is to decide what the future of work looks like, right?
